title: Inferring meaning: reading between the lines
canonical_examples_source: Language rules self-verified; format ref: bank uk-ks2-2024-gps (KS2 GPS).

blocks.content: Writers do not say everything directly. Good readers make inferences — smart guesses from the clues in the text plus what they already know.
An inference is a smart guess made from clues in the text plus what you already know.
Read this: 'Maya grabbed her umbrella and rushed out, glancing up at the grey, heavy sky.'

blocks.question: What can you infer from the clues?
options: It is a bright, sunny day.
blocks.explain: An umbrella and a grey, heavy sky are clues that it might rain — even though the text does not say so directly.
blocks.rule: An inference is a smart guess from clues in the text plus what you already know.

practiceItems.prompt: reading between the lines to guess is making an ___
an inference uses clues and what you already ___
a grey sky and an umbrella suggest it might ___
an inference is a smart ___ from clues

blocks.content: To infer, gather the clues the writer gives, then add your own knowledge of the world.

blocks.question: 'Ravi's stomach growled loudly as he stared at the clock.' What can you infer?
blocks.explain: A growling stomach is a clue that Ravi is hungry.
blocks.rule: Combine the text's clues with what you know to infer what is really happening.

practiceItems.prompt: a growling stomach is a clue that someone is ___
yawning and rubbing eyes suggests someone is ___
to infer, you combine clues with your own ___
an inference is not stated ___ in the text (directly/never)

blocks.content: Gather the clues, add what you know, and make your smart guess. That is inferring. Let's practise!
